exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```clojure
(ns geo.core)
(prn ::lat)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. The double colon is reader shorthand; the keyword itself is fully qualified. With which namespace?
Not yet. The double colon adds a namespace to the keyword.

hints: `::name` is qualified with the current namespace.
exercises.solution: It prints **`:geo.core/lat`**. The reader expands `::lat` using the namespace in effect, `geo.core`. Qualified keywords keep keys from different parts of a system from colliding.

exercises.prompt: With the source path `src`, in which file must the namespace `my-app.http-server` live?

options.label: `src/my-app/http-server.clj`
options.feedback: Not yet. Hyphens are not valid in Java package and class names, so they become underscores in file paths.

options.label: `src/my_app/http_server.clj`
options.feedback: Yes. Dots become directories and hyphens become underscores.

options.label: `src/my_app.http_server.clj`
options.feedback: Not yet. Each dot-separated part except the last is a directory.

options.label: Any file, as long as it starts with `(ns my-app.http-server)`.
options.feedback: Not yet. `require` finds a namespace by turning its name into a path on the classpath, so the location matters.

hints: `require` converts the namespace name to a path: dots to slashes, and one more character substitution.
exercises.solution: **`src/my_app/http_server.clj`**. `require` maps dots to directory separators and hyphens to underscores (because the namespace compiles to Java classes, whose names cannot contain hyphens), then looks for the file on the classpath.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```clojure
(defmulti greet :lang)
(defmethod greet :fr [_] "Bonjour")
(defmethod greet :default [_] "Hello")

(println (greet {:lang :fr}) (greet {:lang :de}) (greet {}))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. For `{}` the dispatch value is `nil`. Is there a method for `nil`, and if not, which one runs?

hints: The dispatch function is `:lang`. What does `(:lang {})` return?
When no method matches the dispatch value, the `:default` method runs.
exercises.solution: It prints **`Bonjour Hello Hello`**. The dispatch values are `:fr`, `:de` and `nil`. Only `:fr` has its own method; the other two fall through to `:default`. Without a `:default` method, the last two calls would throw an `IllegalArgumentException` saying there is no method for that dispatch value.

exercises.prompt: You need a `to-json` operation that works on your own records and also on Java's `String`, `Long` and `java.time.Instant`, and it is called millions of times per second. Which tool fits best?

options.label: A protocol, extended to each type with `extend-protocol`.
options.feedback: Yes. Dispatch is on the type of the first argument, you can extend Java classes you did not write, and protocol calls are fast.

options.label: A multimethod dispatching on `:type`.
options.feedback: Not yet. A `String` or `Instant` has no `:type` key. A multimethod on `class` would work, but it is slower than a protocol for pure type dispatch.

options.label: A `cond` with one branch per type inside a single function.
options.feedback: Not yet. It works, but it is closed: nobody can add a new type without editing the function.

options.label: A record for each Java type.
options.feedback: Not yet. You cannot turn existing Java classes into records; records are new types.

hints: The dispatch is purely on the type of the first argument, and speed matters.
exercises.solution: A **protocol**. It dispatches on the type of its first argument using the JVM's own machinery, which is fast, and `extend-protocol` can add implementations for classes you did not write (`String`, `Long`, `Instant`) as well as your records. Multimethods shine when dispatch depends on values in the data rather than on types.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print?

```clojure
(defrecord P [x y])
(prn (:x (->P 1 2)) (map? (->P 1 2)) (count (assoc (->P 1 2) :z 3)))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. Records accept extra keys through `assoc`. How many keys does the result have?
Not yet. Records implement Clojure's map interfaces, so `map?` is true.

hints: Records behave like maps: keyword lookup, `assoc`, `count` all work.
exercises.solution: It prints **`1 true 3`**. Keywords look up record fields, `map?` is true because records implement the map interfaces, and `assoc` of a new key `:z` gives a record with three keys. (Removing one of the declared fields with `dissoc`, by contrast, gives back a plain map, since the result no longer fits the record's shape.)

exercises.prompt:
With `clojure.spec.alpha` required as `s`, what does this print?

```clojure
(prn (s/conform (s/or :n int? :s string?) "hi"))
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `s/conform` on an `s/or` spec tells you which branch matched.
Not yet. That is `s/valid?`. `s/conform` returns the parsed value.

hints: An `s/or` spec conforms to a vector of the matching branch's tag and the value.
exercises.solution: It prints **`[:s "hi"]`**. `s/conform` parses the value: for an `s/or`, it returns the tag of the branch that matched together with the value, so code can branch on `:n` or `:s` without re-testing. Invalid input would give `:clojure.spec.alpha/invalid`.

options.label: `true`
options.feedback: Yes. Spec maps are open: unknown keys are allowed, and only the specified keys are checked.

options.label: `false`, because `:extra` is not in the spec.
options.feedback: Not yet. Spec deliberately allows keys it does not mention, so that data can grow without breaking consumers.

options.label: An exception, because `:extra` has no spec.
options.feedback: Not yet. Keys without a registered spec are simply not checked.

hints: Are spec's map descriptions open or closed?
exercises.solution: It returns **`true`**. The required unqualified key `:a` is present and is an integer. `:extra` is not mentioned and has no registered spec, so it is ignored. Spec's designers made maps open on purpose: a consumer should not break because a producer added a field.

exercises.prompt: Your service receives configuration text from a file that users can upload. How should it parse the text?

options.label: `clojure.edn/read-string`
options.feedback: Yes. The EDN reader only reads data; it cannot be made to evaluate code.

options.label: `clojure.core/read-string`
options.feedback: Not yet. The full Clojure reader supports features that can run code, so it must never see untrusted input.

options.label: `eval` on the text
options.feedback: Not yet. That would run whatever code the user uploaded.

hints: One of these readers exists precisely for data from outside your program.
exercises.solution: Use **`clojure.edn/read-string`** (or `clojure.edn/read` on a reader). EDN is the data subset of Clojure's syntax, and the EDN reader never evaluates anything, so it is safe for untrusted input. `clojure.core/read-string` is meant for reading code you trust.
